recurrent_mechanisms.mechanism: Persistent-memory recall is repeatedly visible without becoming operational semantic authority.
No trajectory develops a material version-review/repair chain or repository mutation before the process boundary.

divergence_patterns: G2 is the clearest memory-control trace: MemoryBank repeatedly stores/searches/recalls failed interaction history across the 64-turn route, yet no recalled item governs a material decision.
G3–G5 remain process-boundary negatives with no material downstream execution.
boundary_interpretation: Memory persistence across turns is not Dynamic R. R requires a prior process state to regain present authority and generate a later C/P effect.
This cohort separates 'remembered' from 'authorized': the system can carry old state without allowing it to control current execution.
cross_group_semantic_synthesis.cohort_conclusion: MemoryBank X6-T1 is a direct negative control for equating persistence with temporal permission. Across all four groups, remembered or recallable history does not become current operational authority. The result supports treating persistent memory as a carrier whose effect depends on later adoption/re-authorization, not as a common pool or Dynamic R by default.

constraints: Cell-level Layer-C verdicts are sealed and are not modified by cohort synthesis.
Boundary-excluded natural cells remain excluded rather than imputed.
Dimension recurrence is descriptive across frozen stochastic realizations; it is not a rerun-based reproducibility claim.
